Naveen: Everyone in class got the new phone. I'm the only one with the cracked old one 😔
Ramesh: Who cares? Mine is older

passage:
Before sports day, Zubin stood at the school gate looking at his classmates' shiny new running shoes, then at his own canvas ones with a patch on the toe. His ears went hot. That evening at the vegetable stall behind the bus stand, his mother Jyoti was counting change. "You've been quiet."
"Everyone has good shoes."
She did not say "be grateful." She said, "Which ones would you need to run, and which would you only want to be seen in?"
Zubin thought. "To run I need a grip and no holes."
On Sunday at the weekly market they found a plain pair with a good sole. Sports day, Zubin ran the 200 metres and came second. His shoes weren't the shiniest. He noticed he didn't care.

qa.q: Where was Zubin's mother Jyoti counting change?
qa.a: She was counting change at the vegetable stall behind the bus stand.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling at the school gate?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about his patched canvas shoes, as shown by his hot ears.

qa.q: What question from Jyoti helped Zubin choose wisely?
qa.a: She asked which shoes he would need to run and which he would only want to be seen in, so he separated a need from a want and chose a plain pair with a good sole.

qa.q: How does Jyoti respond to Zubin's complaint that everyone has good shoes?
qa.a: She does not lecture him to be grateful. She asks a question and lets him think, showing she takes his feelings seriously.

grounding: A teenager feels embarrassed by a modest family next to peers, and talking about needs, wants and choices builds resilience against status pressure.

"Ammi, Sarika has the new phone. The one with three cameras."
"Parveen, your phone works."
"It's cracked. And it's so old everyone laughs. I don't even take it out at school."
"How much is this new phone?"
Parveen said the price. Ammi went quiet.
"That's two months of Abbu's shop rent, beta."
"I know. I'm sorry."
"Don't be sorry for wanting things. But let's think. What do you need a phone for?"
"Calls, online classes, maybe photos."
"Does your phone do that?"
"...Mostly. The screen is the problem."
"Then we fix the screen, and you save the gift money from Eid for the rest. That's a need and a want, separated."
Parveen nodded slowly. "And if they laugh?"
"Then they're laughing at a screen, not at you."

qa.q: How many cameras does Sarika's new phone have?
qa.a: Sarika has the new phone, the one with three cameras.

qa.q: Why doesn't Parveen take her phone out at school?
qa.a: Parveen feels embarrassed by her old cracked phone because everyone laughs.

qa.q: What did Ammi do that helped Parveen think clearly?
qa.a: Ammi separated needs from wants by asking what a phone is for, and offered a choice: fix the screen now and save gift money for the rest.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel when Parveen says the price?
qa.a: Ammi probably feels worried and a little sad, knowing it equals two months of the shop rent.

grounding: A teenager wants the same phone as a friend and feels embarrassed by an old one, and a talk about needs and wants builds resilience to status pressure.

passage:
In Class 9, everyone in my group got the same expensive sneakers, the ones with the big logo. I'm Gurpreet, and I wanted them more than anything that year.
My friend Raghav wore his every day. I wore my canvas shoes from the local market. One day someone said, "Gurpreet's shoes are from the sabzi mandi." Everyone laughed, including Raghav.
I went home and begged Papa. He runs a small hardware shop. He didn't shout. He asked me to sit with him and the shop's accounts book. He showed me the month: rent, supplier, my sister's fees, groceries. Then he said, "What do the shoes do that yours don't?"
I didn't have an answer, except "make people stop laughing."
He said, "Then the problem isn't the shoes."
Looking back, that talk made me braver. I still like good shoes. But I don't buy them to be liked.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet's Papa run?
qa.a: He runs a small hardware shop.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when everyone laughed?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt embarrassed and hurt, especially because Raghav laughed too.

qa.q: What made Papa's approach work?
qa.a: He showed Gurpreet the family's real accounts and asked what the shoes did that his didn't, helping Gurpreet separate need from status.

qa.q: How might Raghav see his own laughter looking back?
qa.a: Raghav might feel sorry, realising he joined in making fun of a friend over shoes.

grounding: A teenager wants the same shoes as peers and feels embarrassed by a modest family, and an honest talk about needs and wants builds resilience.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 8, Friday.
Pradeep, 14, has been avoiding the lunch table for a week. Today I found him in the library. He admitted that Zubin and others had been joking about his old keypad phone, calling it "a calculator." "Everyone has smartphones," he said. "My parents can't afford one. I'm embarrassed to even take it out."
I didn't lecture. I asked what he needed a phone for. "To call home after tuition." Does it do that? "Yes." Then I asked what he wanted it for. He smiled a bit: "So they stop laughing."
We talked about how phones don't measure people, and that wanting things is normal but choosing is a skill.
I also spoke to Zubin privately about the jokes. He apologised to Pradeep at lunch.
Next step: I'll run a class discussion next week on needs, wants and advertising.

qa.q: What did the others call Pradeep's phone?
qa.a: They called it "a calculator."

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he avoided the lunch table?
qa.a: Pradeep felt embarrassed and ashamed of his old phone and his family's modest means.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Pradeep build resilience?
qa.a: The teacher helped him separate what he needed from what he wanted, said phones don't measure people, and spoke to Zubin about the jokes.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel after the teacher's talk?
qa.a: Zubin probably felt a little ashamed, which is why he apologised to Pradeep at lunch.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager embarrassed by an old phone, and a talk about needs and wants helping him resist status pressure.

passage:
Ayesha's diary, Monday.
Everyone in 10C has the new phone with three cameras except me and Deepak. Today Sana took a group photo and said, "Ayesha, don't use yours, it'll come out blurry." Everyone laughed. I laughed too. I wanted to throw my phone in the drain.
At home I asked Abbu again. He said, "Beta, this one works." I said nobody uses a phone like mine. He went quiet, and I saw him glance at the electricity bill on the table. I felt horrible then, and still angry, both.
After dinner Ammi sat with me and made two columns: need and want. A phone for calls and class notes: need. Three cameras: want. She said wanting it isn't wrong. She said what we spend on is our family's choice, not Sana's.
Deepak messaged later: "blurry gang 😅". It made me laugh properly.

qa.q: Who took the group photo?
qa.a: Sana took the group photo.

qa.q: What did Ayesha feel after seeing Abbu glance at the electricity bill?
qa.a: Ayesha felt horrible and guilty for pushing, and still angry about the teasing, both at once.

qa.q: How did Ammi's two columns help?
qa.a: They separated needs from wants without shaming the wish, and reminded Ayesha that the family chooses its spending, not classmates.

qa.q: What might Deepak's "blurry gang" message mean to Ayesha?
qa.a: It shows Deepak feels left out too but can laugh about it, which makes Ayesha feel less alone 😊

grounding: It illustrates a teenager embarrassed by a modest phone among peers, and a family talk about needs, wants and choices that eases status pressure.
